construction_pair.name: Construction Pair
construction_pair.description: Two vectors, one answer, and five arguments for it - three drawings, two assertions, and neither vocabulary has both. Three artifacts declare an axis called construction and ask the same question with two different lists: VectorAddition says parallelogram | chain | commute | bare, VectorSubtraction says flip | chain | parallelogram | bare, example_1_3_vector_subtraction_vr says bare | flip | chain | parallelogram. Three members, three different defaults - the only vocabulary in the corpus with no majority reading of itself. Read from the dispatch rather than the prose, the two extra words are both UNIONS of readings the list already has: flip is chain UNION parallelogram (VectorSubtraction:192-197, example_1_3:352-354), commute is chain UNION its own mirror image (VectorAddition:256-261). So the vocabularies differ only in which union they bothered to name, and the historical subtraction build draws one side of its own figure twice - the dotted run on a's tip to the difference is coincident with the solid chained copy, in both subtraction members, under both their defaults. A 0.808 x 0.696 m frame with two feet stands the world box at 0.808 x 0.696 x 0.128 in all ten cells before a single construction rod exists. Inside it two fixed operands - example_1_3's own planar pair, rotated so it photographs square - and the resultant, identical vertex for vertex across all five constructions of a column. The second axis is where the family's unsaid fact lives: a + b is one diagonal of the parallelogram and a - b is the OTHER, and |a+b|^2 + |a-b|^2 = 0.388800 = 2(|a|^2 + |b|^2) exactly. No RandomNumberGenerator, no randf, no noise, no _process, no Timer.
dev_themes: a proof is not a picture
the word that names a union
interactions: stand at construction=parallelogram and walk the operation axis. The two operand arrows do not move; only the answer does, and it swings from one diagonal of the figure to the other. That is the sentence the three members never say together - the sum and the difference are the two diagonals of ONE parallelogram, and the arithmetic is exact here: 0.244800 + 0.144000 = 0.388800 = 2(0.090000 + 0.104400)

compare parallelogram against commute in the add column. Same two segments, drawn twice - dotted in one, solid with heads in the other. The theorem is not a new figure, it is the figure asserted as two journeys instead of one shape, and the resultant is identical in both because the assertion adds no new point

look for `flip` in the add column and for `commute` in the subtract column. Both are exact repeats of `bare`, because addition's vocabulary has no flip and subtraction's has no commute. Those two zeros are the census: the union of two vocabularies has holes, and the holes are measurable

put parallelogram and flip side by side in the subtract column. The only difference is one solid rod laid along a segment that was already dotted - flip does not add a side, it makes one of the parallelogram's four sides solid and buries the dots inside it. That double-draw is not this bench's invention; it is what both subtraction members ship as their default

count the objects at chain in either column: one. The chained copy is the whole of subtraction's `chain` AND the whole of addition's `chain`, and it is inside both unions. It is the only mark all three members agree about
construction_pair.capacity: SEE that a construction is an ARGUMENT and not a style - that a chain claims addition is a journey, a parallelogram claims it is a symmetric fact, and commute and flip are not drawings at all but two different UNIONS of those claims, each named by only one half of a family that teaches one operation twice

spatial_needs.footprint_note: THE FRAME IS THE FOOTPRINT AND IT IS DRAWN BEFORE EITHER AXIS IS CONSULTED: four 0.018 m square rods on outer half-extents 0.404 x 0.348, plus two 0.048 x 0.018 x 0.128 feet at x = +-0.300 that give the piece its only depth. The frame is the reason the AABB is a constant. Without it the box would be a fact about which construction was picked - `bare` draws three arrows and `flip` draws seven objects - the camera would move between cells, and every measured pair would carry a framing difference it did not earn. THE FIGURE INSIDE MOVES A GREAT DEAL AND IS ALLOWED TO: the drawn point set spans 0.489 x 0.378 m in the add column, 0.260 x 0.606 m at bare and chain under subtract, and 0.489 x 0.606 m at the three subtract readings that stand -b at the origin. The world box is 0.808 x 0.696 x 0.128 in every one of the ten cells regardless, and the figure clears the frame's inner opening by at least 0.027 m at every arrowhead - checked at all four extreme heads, including the resultant cone at a+b whose base circle reaches x = 0.3126 against an opening at 0.386. layout=ladder stands all five constructions in a row at 0.90 m pitch, about 4.4 m wide, and is a design view rather than a map placement.

measurements.source: computed_from_geometry from the file's own constants; no Godot was run. The box is the FRAME and its two feet and nothing else. The frame spans x at +-FRAME_HX = 0.404 and y from 0 to 2 x FRAME_HY = 0.696; the feet span z at +-FOOT_D/2 = 0.064, which is more than the widest thing the figure can produce (the resultant arrowhead's base radius, R_RESULT x HEAD_FLARE = 0.052). Every drawn point of every cell lies inside x = +-0.358650 and y = 0.348 +-0.303200 of the frame centre, which is 0.045 m inside the frame on all four sides before arrowheads and at least 0.027 m after them.

dna.default: construction=parallelogram, operation=add. THE DEFAULT HAD TO BE ARGUED FOR, because this is the only vocabulary in the corpus with NO MAJORITY READING OF ITSELF: VectorAddition ships `parallelogram` (gd:31), VectorSubtraction ships `flip` (gd:30), example_1_3 ships `bare` (gd:58). Three members, three different defaults, and each one calls its own the historical build. The tie between the two values that are declared by all three AND shipped by one - parallelogram and bare - is broken on which cell carries the bench's claim: `parallelogram` is the only value whose MEANING changes across the second axis, because the completing sides it draws belong to the figure a and b span under add and to the figure a and -b span under subtract, and the two diagonals of those figures are the sum and the difference of the same pair. `bare` would have made the default cell three arrows and nothing to be wrong about. operation=add because addition is the operation the family teaches first and says so in both directions - VectorAddition's relationships line calls itself `prerequisite to VectorSubtraction`, VectorSubtraction's calls itself the `inverse of VectorAddition` - and because parallelogram is VectorAddition's own default, so the default cell is one member's shipped picture rather than a blend of three.
dna.note:
WHAT THE VALUES MEAN, which member each came from, and whether it is a DRAWING or an ASSERTION. THE FAMILY FIRST, as a census before it is an argument: three artifacts declare an axis called `construction` and it asks the same question in all three - which argument for the combination does this bench actually draw?

  VectorAddition                     parallelogram | chain | commute | bare      default parallelogram
  VectorSubtraction                  flip | chain | parallelogram | bare         default flip
  example_1_3_vector_subtraction_vr  bare | flip | chain | parallelogram         default bare

Three distinct scenes on three distinct scripts, checked. THREE WORDS ARE UNANIMOUS - chain, parallelogram, bare - and the fourth is where the two vocabularies split. example_1_3's own header says the shared words are not synonyms and says why it matters: it took both its word and its value list character for character from VectorSubtraction, and wrote that `a shared vocabulary is only honest if the siblings measure alike`.

THE THING THE CODE SAYS THAT THE BRIEF DID NOT, and it is the finding. The brief said `flip` is subtraction's own move, a - b drawn as a + (-b). IT IS NOT A MOVE. IT IS A UNION, and so is `commute`:

  flip     VectorSubtraction:192-197 makes _shows_flipped_at_origin() return
           _shows_parallelogram(), which is flip-or-parallelogram, and _shows_tip_to_tail()
           flip-or-chain. example_1_3:352-354 says the same in three lines - _want_neg_origin
           = flip or parallelogram, _want_neg_tip = flip or chain, _want_dots = flip or
           parallelogram. So flip = chain UNION parallelogram, exactly, in both members.
           And the negation itself is drawn under `chain` too: the chained copy IS -b, just
           rooted at a's tip rather than at the origin. EVERY NON-BARE VALUE IS A FLIP. The
           word names the union, not the move.
  commute  VectorAddition:256-261 - _shows_chain_b() is chain-or-commute, _shows_chain_a()
           is commute alone. So commute = chain UNION its own mirror image.

THE TWO VOCABULARIES THEREFORE DIFFER BY EXACTLY ONE THING: WHICH UNION THEY BOTHERED TO NAME. Neither member has the other's. That is the whole content of the split, and it is why this axis is worth a bench.

AND THE PARALLELOGRAM AND THE TWO CHAINS ARE THE SAME TWO SEGMENTS. VectorAddition's dotted_line_a runs a -> result and dotted_line_b runs b -> result (:352-354); its chain_b_at_a sits at a and spans b, its chain_a_at_b sits at b and spans a (:199-203). Those are the same two segments. `parallelogram` draws them DOTTED, `commute` draws them SOLID WITH HEADS. THE THEOREM IS NOT A NEW FIGURE - it is the figure asserted as two journeys instead of one shape, and that is what makes it an assertion rather than a drawing.

A SMALLER CODE FINDING, KEPT BECAUSE IT IS A COLOUR TRAP: VectorAddition colours the two dotted runs by the WRONG operand. dotted_line_a is coral, a's colour, and runs from a's tip - but the segment from a's tip is the copy of B, and the floating label sitting on it says `b (copy)` (:148-149, :207-209). Labels right, colours crossed. This bench colours each copy for what it IS a copy of, and both copies share one chalk so that `commute`'s two arrows read as two instances of one claim.

CONSTRUCTION, five values, the union of the two lists in the order example_1_3 declares the shared three, with each vocabulary's own extra word last.

  bare           DRAWING, and the null. The three arrows and nothing else - a, b and the
                 answer. Declared by all three members and shipped by example_1_3, whose
                 header calls it `THE SHIPPED BUILD, byte for byte - outside bare not one
                 construction node is ever created`. The claim is left to the arrows.
  chain          DRAWING. The second operand re-rooted at a's tip: one walk, out along a
                 and then on along q, landing on the answer. Declared by all three and
                 shipped by NONE, which is the only value in the vocabulary nobody
                 defaults to. It is the value that makes order look like it matters,
                 because a journey has a first leg.
  parallelogram  DRAWING. The two completing sides of the figure a and q span, as dotted
                 runs, and under subtract the arrow -b standing at the origin as well -
                 which is exactly the gate both subtraction members put on it. The claim
                 is that the answer is a diagonal of a figure, so order cannot matter,
                 because a figure has no first side. VectorAddition's default.
  flip           ASSERTION, and subtraction's word. chain AND parallelogram at once, with
                 the dotted run on a -> r BURIED inside the solid copy laid over it -
                 which is not a flourish, it is what both subtraction members do:
                 VectorSubtraction's dotted_line_neg_b runs head -> diff (:148) while
                 tip_tail_neg_b sits at head and spans -tail (:142-143), the same segment;
                 example_1_3 repeats it at :442 and :446. Both ship that double-draw as
                 their default. VectorSubtraction's default. ABSENT FROM ADDITION'S LIST.
  commute        ASSERTION, and addition's word. Both chains - q at a's tip and a at q's
                 tip - two different journeys landing on the same point, which is what
                 a + b = b + a actually claims. It adds no new point to the picture, only
                 new furniture, and the resultant arrow is identical to chain's and to
                 parallelogram's by construction. ABSENT FROM SUBTRACTION'S LIST.

A VALUE A COLUMN'S VOCABULARY DOES NOT DECLARE IS DRAWN AS AN ABSENCE. That is component_court's rule for the same situation in the same domain - vector_magnitude_demo declares only star, chain and none, and `that subset is honest and is drawn as an absence`. So `flip` under add and `commute` under subtract are exact repeats of `bare`, and those two zeros are the census made measurable: the union of two vocabularies has holes, and here is what they weigh.

OPERATION, two values, because the family has exactly two and there is no third operation anywhere in the three files.

  add       q = b, the answer is a + b. VectorAddition's whole subject.
  subtract  q = -b, the answer is a + (-b) = a - b. VectorSubtraction's and example_1_3's
            subject, and their own identity line for it: `a - b = a + (-b)`. The bench
            computes a + q in both columns from one line, which is that identity written
            once instead of argued about.

AND THE SECOND AXIS IS WHERE THE FAMILY'S UNSAID FACT LIVES. Under add the answer is the parallelogram's diagonal from the origin. Under subtract it is THE OTHER DIAGONAL OF THE SAME PARALLELOGRAM - the one running from b's tip to a's tip, which is precisely what VectorSubtraction's @identity line 8 says the difference is (`a-b always points from b's tip to a's tip`) and which no member has ever drawn in the same picture as the sum. So `parallelogram` does not mean the same thing in the two columns, and that is a geometric fact rather than a presentation choice. The arithmetic is exact at these operands: |a+b|^2 = 0.244800, |a-b|^2 = 0.144000, sum 0.388800, and 2(|a|^2 + |b|^2) = 2(0.090000 + 0.104400) = 0.388800. The parallelogram law, to six figures, on the family's own pair.

THE OPERANDS ARE example_1_3'S OWN, RIGIDLY ROTATED, and the choice of member is forced rather than aesthetic. Its pair is the only PLANAR one in the family - vector_a = (0.2, 0.15, 0), vector_b = (-0.1, 0.25, 0), z exactly zero, because it is Shiffman's 2D original translated - and a plane is not a simplification of this operation but its own shape: a and b span a plane and every one of a + b, a - b, -b and both parallelograms lies inside it. Nothing is flattened. The rotation is -66.8699 degrees, which puts a at exactly -30 degrees and b at 44.9315; it preserves the angle between the operands (74.9315 degrees) and the length ratio |b|/|a| = 1.077033 to six figures, and it is chosen for one measurable reason - at the capture standpoint world x projects to (0.8139, -0.1494) and world y to (0, 0.9665), so a figure must be 1.187 times wider than tall to photograph square, and the union box is 1.1829. The scale puts |a| at exactly 0.300 m. The other two members' pairs were measured too and are in `declines`.

HOW THE SHEET IS PROTECTED FROM THE COLOUR TRAP, and it matters here more than usual: all three members carry the entire distinction in HUE - coral against cyan, pink against green - while the critic measures luminance by default and has only a separate per-channel rescue. A sheet built the members' way would read as five twins in greyscale. The Rec.709 ladder here is frame 0.301, operand b 0.438, operand a 0.575, copy 0.728, resultant 0.860; no two things that must be told apart sit within 0.13 of each other. THE ONE DELIBERATE COLLISION is that -b is drawn in b's exact colour and exact weight, because -b IS b turned around and the two can never be confused - they leave the same origin in opposite directions. The members give the negative its own pink, which says it is a third object; the code says it is not.

THE THESIS SOMEONE COULD DISAGREE WITH: two of these five values are not drawings at all. chain, parallelogram and bare are three claims about what addition IS; flip and commute are unions of those claims, and a union is an assertion about the other values rather than a picture of the operation. A family that puts a theorem inside a list of drawing styles has hidden a proof in a dropdown. THE DISAGREEMENT AVAILABLE, and it is fair: a reader can say a union IS a drawing - it puts ink on the page, it can be photographed, and showing two arguments at once is a perfectly good third argument. The answer is in the pixels this bench will produce: `commute` adds not one point that `chain` and `parallelogram` do not already have, and `flip` adds one side of its own figure twice. The cell where holding the thesis costs something is `flip` under subtract, where the buried run means the sheet cannot show the difference between drawing a side once and drawing it twice - the redundancy is real, and invisible.

predicted_degeneracy.pair: parallelogram against flip, in the add operation
predicted_degeneracy.arithmetic:
THE CONTEXT IS THE `add` COLUMN AND THE RANKING IS COMPUTED INSIDE IT. Ten pairs over five values, one of which is a designed null (flip = bare). Ranked by changed projected area, in square metres of the capture plane: parallelogram-flip 0.004695 (the named pair, and identical to parallelogram-bare because flip IS bare in this column), bare-chain 0.007707, chain-parallelogram 0.007363, chain-commute 0.008267, parallelogram-commute 0.010684, bare-commute 0.016026. The named pair is the smallest in the column AND the smallest non-null anywhere in the sheet - every cross-axis pair redraws the resultant arrow, which is 0.0155-0.0164 m2 on its own.

WHY THAT PAIR IS THE FLOOR, AND IT IS BY CONSTRUCTION. VectorAddition declares no `flip`, so under `add` that cell draws exactly what `bare` draws: the three arrows and nothing else. `parallelogram` adds two dotted runs and NOTHING ELSE - no arrow, no head, no rod. The entire difference between the two frames is 13 small cubes.

THE NUMBER. Run one, a's tip to a+b, is 0.323110 m long, so n = int(0.323110 / 0.040) + 1 = 9 dots at t = i/8; run two, b's tip to a+b, is 0.300000 m long, so n = 8. TWO DOTS OF EACH RUN LAND INSIDE AN ARROWHEAD THAT IS ALREADY THERE - one at the operand's tip, one at the resultant's tip - so 7 + 6 = 13 dots are visible, not 17. A 0.015 m cube seen along the capture direction (0.5615, 0.2571, 0.7866) has a silhouette of side^2 x (|dx| + |dy| + |dz|) = 0.000225 x 1.6052 = 0.00036117 m2, and at 0.040 m spacing against a projected dot width of about 0.018 m no two overlap. 13 x 0.00036117 = 0.004695 m2.

THE DENOMINATOR IS THE CROP, NOT THE FRAME. Camera is capture_config_sweep's - FOV 34, PAD 1.9, yaw 0.62, pitch -0.26, 760 x 760 - with framing 0.58 on an AABB of 0.808 x 0.696 x 0.128, diagonal 1.074087, so the frame is 1.074087 x 1.9 x 0.58 = 1.18365 m across in every cell. Screen basis at that standpoint: x-hat -> (0.8139, -0.1494), y-hat -> (0, 0.9665), z-hat -> (-0.5811, -0.2093). The stage projects to 0.732012 m wide by 0.820190 m tall, which is 470 x 527 px of the 760 and is IDENTICAL in both frames because the frame and feet are identical, so the critic's crop to the union of the two subject boxes is that box. Crop area 0.600377 m2. Changed fraction 0.004695 / 0.600377 = 0.782 percent, which over the critic's 160 x 160 = 25600 px resize is 200 px.

200 IS WELL UNDER THE 1280-PIXEL FOCUS WINDOW, so the window does NOT fill and the number is set by area as well as contrast - the opposite of cohort_bench's case, and the reason this prediction is small. Contrast: the copy chalk is Rec.709 0.728 against a neutralised background of about 0.10, so 0.628 x 255 = 160, times the 0.77 lighting-and-tonemap compression the substance_room replica measured = 123. One more factor applies here and did not there: the crop is downscaled 2.9x to 160 x 160, and a dot that is about 11 px across in the render lands at 3.7 px after it, so the box filter softens its edges - measured on comparable features at about 0.85 retention, giving an effective 105. focus = (200 x 105 + 1080 x 4) / (1280 x 255) = 25320 / 326400 = 7.76 percent. Registered at 7.6. Frame-wide: 25320 / 6528000 = 0.39 percent.

THE CROSS-CHECK THAT MAKES THIS PREDICTION WORTH MAKING. The SAME NAMED PAIR exists in the other column and should measure DIFFERENTLY, for a different reason: under subtract, `flip` is declared, so parallelogram-against-flip there is one solid copy rod laid along a run that was already dotted. That rod is 0.008307 m2, it buries 7 dots worth 0.002528 m2 in its own colour, and about 0.000385 m2 of its head hides inside the resultant's head, leaving 0.005394 m2 = 230 px, and at 6.5 px wide the downscale costs it less (0.95, effective 117): 9.53 percent. So the prediction is really two numbers, 7.6 and 9.5, a ratio of 1.25, and the pair that is a two-run absence in one column is a buried rod in the other.

THE PREDICTION IS A FLOOR, NOT A FORECAST. The replica has one key, flat shading, no shadows, no AO, no antialiasing and no emission, and every prior prediction in this corpus under-read by 1.5x to 6.7x; the emission multipliers here (0.7 on the copies) are not modelled at all and push the true contrast up. IF THE SWEEP COMES BACK BELOW 7.6 ON THE NAMED PAIR, STOP AND INVESTIGATE THE HARNESS BEFORE THE DESIGN: (a) tools/check_dna_declarations.py, because a value the code cannot reach falls back to the default and prints identical tiles; (b) _rejects.json, because all three exports are String enums and Object.set() on a typed property of the wrong type is refused in SILENCE; (c) whether the sheet was captured with --max=10, because at build_dna_gallery's default cap of 9 the 5 x 2 cross product is trimmed from the tail of the LATER axis and `operation` collapses to [add] alone, which deletes the entire subtract column, one of the two designed nulls, the cross-check above and the whole second axis.

designed_nulls.why: IDENTICAL BY CONSTRUCTION, AND IT IS HALF THE CENSUS. VectorAddition's enum is (parallelogram, chain, commute, bare). It has no `flip`, and its own apply_grid_config refuses one - `if c in CONSTRUCTION_VALUES` at gd:314 - so a map token asking that member for flip changes nothing at all. This bench draws that as an absence, which is component_court's rule for the same situation in the same domain (vector_magnitude_demo declares no `box`; that subset is honest and is drawn as an absence). _build_figure returns immediately after the three invariant arrows, so the two frames are the same frame, the same feet, the same a, the same b, the same a+b, and no construction node exists in either. Predicted 0.00 percent focus and 0.00 percent frame. Anything above 0.5 percent is render noise; anything above 2 percent means the absence gate is not firing and `flip` is drawing subtraction's union in a column that has no word for it, which would make the prediction above - whose whole basis is that flip IS bare here - a fact about a broken gate.

THE OTHER HALF OF THE SAME CENSUS, AND IT IS THE SHARPER ONE. VectorSubtraction's enum is (flip, chain, parallelogram, bare) and example_1_3's is (bare, flip, chain, parallelogram); NEITHER has `commute`, and both refuse it at the config hook (VectorSubtraction:325, example_1_3:286). So the subtract column draws nothing for it. WHAT MAKES THIS ONE SHARP IS THAT THE THING IS TRUE AND STILL HAS NO WORD: a + (-b) = (-b) + a holds exactly, because ADDITION commutes even where subtraction does not, and the two chained copies would land on the same tip. Subtraction's non-commutativity - a - b != b - a - is a claim about swapping the OPERANDS, which is these members' `order` axis and not this one, and the family has quietly let the two questions share a shadow. Predicted 0.00 percent. Anything above 0.5 percent is render noise; above 2 percent means the gate is not firing. THE CONTRAST THAT MUST HOLD ALONGSIDE BOTH NULLS: `commute` under add and `flip` under subtract must be among the LOUDEST cells in their columns - 0.016026 and 0.018949 m2 of change against bare respectively - because each draws its vocabulary's full union. Two zeros and two peaks, on the same two words, in opposite columns.

dna.designed_nulls_why: TWO NULLS, ONE FACT, AND IT IS THE ARGUMENT RATHER THAN A CHECK ON IT. The only pairs in this sheet that are identical by construction are the two vocabulary holes, and they say the thing the bench exists to say: two artifact families teach one operation with one word and four values, and the fourth value is a different word in each - so the union of their vocabularies is five long and every reading of it is missing one. FOUR OTHER NULLS WERE CONSIDERED AND ARE NOT CONSTRUCTIBLE, recorded rather than quietly dropped. (1) bare@add against bare@subtract: the two operand arrows are identical but the answer is the other diagonal, 0.494773 m against 0.379473 m in a direction 84 degrees away, so it is one of the widest pairs in the sheet rather than the narrowest. (2) commute against parallelogram: the brief's suggestion, and it is a near-miss rather than a null - they occupy exactly the same two segments and differ only in dotted against solid-with-heads, which is 0.010684 m2, the fourth-widest pair in the add column. The equality is real but it is an equality of POSITION, and it is registered as predicted_relationship instead, where it can be tested by a mask rather than by a diff. (3) the buried dotted run under `flip`: the dots on a -> r sit strictly inside the copy rod laid over them (worst-case corner distance 0.0075 x sqrt(3) = 0.012990 m against a rod radius of 0.015), so they contribute exactly zero pixels - a true designed identity, but between an object and itself rather than between two variants, so it cannot be written as a pair. It is the sharpest thing this bench knows and the sheet cannot show it. (4) an a perpendicular to b, which would make |a+b| = |a-b| exactly and the two columns congruent: refused, because the two figures would be MIRROR IMAGES rather than the same image, and because orthogonality is VectorAddition's `pair` axis (gd:45), a third question this bench does not ask.
dna.predicted_relationship: THE ANSWER NEVER MOVES, and it is falsifiable without reference to any percentage. The three arrows - a, b and the resultant - are drawn in _build_figure BEFORE the construction branch and no branch below touches them, which is exactly how all three members are built (VectorAddition applies construction as pure visibility on nodes the sum vector is not among; VectorSubtraction's _apply_construction touches only negative_b, tip_tail_neg_b, the dotted lines and their labels; example_1_3's three shipped arrows are `never hidden, never re-styled and never re-scaled by any of this`, gd:53-55). FALSIFYING TEST: take the subject mask of the `bare` frame of a column - which contains the frame, the feet and exactly those three arrows - and ask what fraction of it survives in the other four frames of the same column. It must be 100.00 percent in all four, twice. Anything less means a construction branch is moving the answer, and every number in this sheet would then be a fact about a moving target. THE STRONGER FORM, AND IT IS THE THESIS: `commute` draws two chained copies that both terminate on the resultant's tip, so the assertion adds NO NEW POINT to the picture - only new furniture. If the mask test passes at commute, that is the theorem verified pixel-exact: two different journeys, one destination, and the destination was already drawn before either journey existed.
dna.fixture_why: The bench can stand all five constructions in a row (layout=ladder, 0.90 m pitch, about 4.4 m wide) but the SWEEP must see one at a time: capture_config_sweep unions the AABB across a spec's variants, so a five-wide row in the same spec would frame every single cell against four and a half metres and photograph the 0.015 m rods and 0.015 m dots as hairs - which is precisely the failure example_1_3 measured and wrote into its own header at gd:102-109, where 6 mm marks made two genuinely different figures differ by 0.045 percent of the frame. layout is an export and not an axis, and it ships at single, so the fixture is a belt over braces. WHAT IS NOT FIXTURED, AND WHY NOTHING NEEDS TO BE: there is no clock and no draw here at all. There is no RandomNumberGenerator in the file, no randf, no FastNoiseLite, no NoiseTexture2D, no _process, no Timer and no tween; every vertex is arithmetic on six constants. That matters because the sources are the opposite of quiet - all three run _process every frame, two of them recompute the whole figure from live grab-sphere positions so that what a still shows is a fact about where a player last left a tip, and VectorAddition additionally builds a physics gadget (RigidBody3D + SliderJoint3D) whose transforms go non-finite under a scaled parent, which is why that member gates it on scale_multiplier <= 2.0. This bench has no time domain to refuse.
dna.kin: COMPONENT_COURT IS THE NEAR KIN AND THE DIFFERENCE IS EXACT: it is the UNARY bench and this is the BINARY one. component_court (wave 13, same category) sweeps `decomposition` over basis_vectors_rig, force_cube and two others - chain, star, box, none - and its subject is ONE vector taken apart into three basis components, an analysis. Its `chain` walks the three COMPONENTS OF ONE VECTOR tip to tail (origin -> x -> xy -> tip) and its invariant is the tip: the components are solved by Cramer's rule so that u+v+w equals RESULTANT at every obliquity, and the whole court asks what a single arrow is made of. This bench's `chain` concatenates TWO INDEPENDENT OPERANDS that were given, not derived, and its subject is what two vectors make, a synthesis. Three consequences follow and none of them exists in the court. (1) The second axis: component_court's is `obliquity`, the shear of the basis, which is only a question when there IS a basis; this one's is `operation`, which is only a question when there are two operands. (2) The values: `commute` and `flip` have no analogue in decomposition, because commutativity is a statement about two arguments and a decomposition has one. (3) The claim: the court's box has a body diagonal that IS the vector; this bench's parallelogram has TWO diagonals and they are the sum and the difference - which is the sentence neither bench's family states and only a binary bench can. WHAT THEY SHARE IS THE WORD `chain` AND THE SHAPE OF THE QUESTION, and that is worth having twice rather than once: the corpus can now ask whether one word means the same thing when the thing being chained is a component and when it is an operand. It does not quite - the court's chain has a canonical order (x then y then z) that the basis supplies, while this one's order is exactly what `commute` denies matters. TWO SMALLER KIN. handed_pair sweeps `handedness` over VectorCrossProduct and is the other binary operation on two vectors, the one whose answer leaves the plane; a room holding both says that two vectors make three things - a sum, a difference and a perpendicular - and that the first two live in their plane. vector_addition_walk and vector_addition_demo are unswept siblings of the same operation and are the first place to look if this axis ever needs a fourth member.
declines: THE BRIEF'S READING OF `flip`, corrected from the code, and it is the biggest change. The brief said flip is subtraction's own move, a - b drawn as a + (-b), and therefore a drawing alongside chain and parallelogram. The dispatch says otherwise in both members that have it: _shows_flipped_at_origin() returns _shows_parallelogram() and _shows_tip_to_tail() is flip-or-chain (VectorSubtraction:192-197), and example_1_3 spells the same three flags at :352-354. flip = chain UNION parallelogram. The negation is not what flip adds - the chained copy under plain `chain` is already -b, just rooted at a's tip - so every non-bare value is a flip and the word names the union. That makes the axis three drawings and TWO assertions rather than four drawings and one, which is the sentence the bench is built to photograph.

A THIRD `operation` VALUE. Three were considered. `both` - draw a+b and a-b on one figure, the two diagonals at once - is the sharpest thing the bench could say and was refused because it makes `operation` two questions in one word (which operation, and how many at a time), which is wave 19's finding about axes that are two axes wearing one word; the two-diagonal fact is carried by the CONTRAST between the two columns instead, where a reader has to do the work. `negate` - relabel the second operand as -b and call the whole thing an addition - was refused because it is the same operation under a different name, which is precisely what `construction` already carries: `flip` IS the relabelling, and putting it in `operation` too would let one claim be measured twice and counted as two. `reverse` (b - a) was refused because it is these members' `order` axis (VectorSubtraction gd:39, example_1_3 gd:59), a real third question that belongs to them and not here. The family has exactly two operations and the axis has exactly two values.

BUILDING `flip` UNDER ADD AND `commute` UNDER SUBTRACT AS HONEST EXTENSIONS. Both are perfectly well defined - flip under add would be the solid chained copy plus both dotted closures, commute under subtract would be the two chains to a-b plus -b at the origin - and drawing them would have given ten distinct pictures instead of eight. Refused, and the refusal is the sheet's only source of exact nulls. The corpus's established rule for a vocabulary gap is component_court's: a value a member does not declare is drawn as an ABSENCE, not invented for it. Inventing here would also have destroyed the finding it was meant to display, because the interesting fact is not what flip under addition WOULD look like - it is that addition never named it and named a theorem instead.

THE OTHER TWO MEMBERS' OPERAND PAIRS, measured before example_1_3's was taken. VectorAddition ships a = (1.8, 0.6, -0.2) and b = (0.4, 1.6, 0.9): |a| = 1.9105, |b| = 1.9000, 65.6 degrees apart, genuinely 3D. VectorSubtraction ships a = (1.6, 0.7, -0.4) and b = (-0.3, 1.1, 0.8): a.b = -0.03, which is 91.2 degrees - the subtraction bench is teaching the operation on an ESSENTIALLY ORTHOGONAL pair, and orthogonality is a special case its sibling declares as a separate axis value (VectorAddition's pair = oblique | orthogonal | parallel | opposed). example_1_3's pair is the only planar one, is 74.9 degrees apart - between the other two - and has |b|/|a| = 1.077, closest of the three to unity. It was taken for the plane rather than for the angle, and the plane is not a simplification: a and b span one, and a+b, a-b, -b and both parallelograms all lie inside it.

A BACK PANEL BEHIND THE FIGURE. It would raise the readability of every mark and was refused twice over: the members draw arrows in empty space and a panel is furniture the family does not have, and a large invariant mid-grey behind the marks LOWERS their contrast (0.728 against a 0.20 panel instead of against a 0.10 backdrop) while adding nothing the frame does not already do for the AABB. The cost is accepted and named: this bench is SPARSE - about 14 percent of the crop carries ink - so verify_batch will read it as sparse-not-small, exactly as it read component_court, and the correct response is not to tighten the framing.

THIN MARKS, WHICH IS COMPONENT_COURT'S ONE MEASURED WEAKNESS AND IS NOT REPEATED. That bench drew this family with 0.009 m legs and 0.004 m box edges and peaked at 1.41 percent of frame - legible to a reader and nearly nothing to the critic, because after the crop and the resize to 160 x 160 those marks are 1.5 to 3.5 px. example_1_3 hit the same wall independently and wrote it into its own header: 6 mm rods made `chain` and `parallelogram` differ by 0.045 percent, `two genuinely different figures that no one could tell apart`, and it doubled them. The weights here are 0.015 to 0.020 m on a 0.72 m figure, about 4 to 6.5 px after the pipeline. THE HONEST COST: these three artifacts really are made of thin arrows, and a bench that fattens them is measuring a slightly different family. It is done anyway, because the alternative is a sheet that cannot be wrong about anything.

CLASS COLOUR AS THE MEMBERS USE IT. All three carry the entire distinction in hue - VectorAddition coral against cyan, VectorSubtraction orange against blue against pink, example_1_3 three shades of one pink from a shared material set - and the critic measures luminance by default. Rebuilt here on a luminance ladder with no two separable things within 0.13. The one place the members' own convention is corrected rather than kept is VectorAddition's crossed dotted-line colours (:142-143 against :207-209), where the run from a's tip is coloured for a and labelled for b.

ANIMATION, AND EVERY RATE, PHASE AND LIVE HANDLE. All three members recompute their figure in _process from live positions - VectorAddition and VectorSubtraction read grab-sphere world positions every frame, so what a still shows is a fact about where a player last left a tip, and example_1_3 reads three parameter controllers. None of that is an axis in any of them and none of it could be: a rate is invisible to a still. This bench has no time domain to refuse, and that is not a stylistic preference - it is the reason two builds of one cell are the same mesh and the reason a diff between two cells means anything at all.

A SECOND SEGMENT FOR THE PARALLELOGRAM'S OTHER TWO SIDES. The figure a and q span has four sides and the members draw only two of them dotted, because the other two ARE the operand arrows, already standing. Keeping to two is faithful and it is also what makes the buried run legible as a redundancy rather than as one of four: under `flip` the members lay a solid copy along one of exactly two dotted sides, so half of the closure they claim is drawn twice.
dna.sweep_note: THE FULL SHEET NEEDS --max=10 AND THE COST OF GETTING IT WRONG IS THE WHOLE SECOND AXIS. `construction` is declared first and is never trimmed; `operation` is second, and build_dna_gallery trims the LATER axis from the tail until the cross product fits its cap. At the default --max=9 the 5 x 2 sheet renders as 5 x 1 = `add` only, which deletes the entire subtract column - and with it one of the two designed nulls, the cross-check that makes the prediction worth making, the -b arrow, the other diagonal, and every cell where `flip` draws anything. What survives is a finished-looking five-tile row in which one tile is silently a repeat of another and nothing can be wrong. Only 10 carries the experiment.
